nameStory: The snakeblenny gets its name from its long, slender body that undulates through the water like a snake swimming through the sea. Unlike true eels, this fish belongs to the prickleback family, but its serpentine movement and elongated form earned it this reptilian comparison.
description: The snakeblenny is a long, thin fish that looks remarkably like a small sea snake as it glides through northern Atlantic waters. This unusual fish has an eel-like body but is actually a type of prickleback, with a continuous fin running along much of its back and belly. Snakeblennies are relatively small fish, typically measuring less than a foot in length, with smooth, scaleless skin that feels slippery to the touch.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely elongated and snake-like, with a body that's much longer than it is tall or wide, feeling smooth and muscular when handled

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long dorsal fin runs continuously along most of the back, paired with a similar anal fin along the belly, creating a ribbon-like appearance

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Usually brownish or olive-colored with darker mottled patterns that help it blend with rocky bottom habitats

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small terminal mouth positioned at the front tip of the pointed head, designed for picking at small prey

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically under 12 inches long but very thin, giving it an almost string-like appearance when swimming

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in cold, rocky coastal waters where it can weave between crevices and under rocks

habitat: Snakeblennies inhabit the cold, rocky coastal waters of northern New England, particularly in Maine's deeper offshore areas. They prefer rocky bottoms and crevices where they can hide among the stones and kelp, typically in waters deeper than most shore fishing spots. These fish are more commonly encountered by commercial fishermen or deep-water anglers than by casual observers.

seasonality.spring: Snakeblennies become more active as waters begin to warm, though they remain in deeper areas. This is when they may start moving toward spawning areas.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're feeding heavily on small crustaceans and marine worms. Breeding typically occurs during warmer months in their deep-water habitat.
seasonality.fall: Continue feeding actively to build reserves for winter, remaining in their rocky deep-water haunts as coastal waters begin to cool.
seasonality.winter: Less active in the coldest months but don't migrate, instead staying deep where temperatures remain more stable year-round.

funFact: Despite looking exactly like a tiny sea snake, snakeblennies are completely harmless fish that are more closely related to sculpins and other bottom-dwelling fish than to any actual snake or eel!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with small eels or lamprey, but snakeblennies have the distinctive continuous dorsal and anal fins that eels lack, and they don't have the circular suction-cup mouth of a lamprey. Remember: if it looks like a snake but has ribbon-like fins, it's probably a snakeblenny.
contextualKnowledge: The snakeblenny belongs to the prickleback family, but despite the family name, this particular species doesn't have the prominent spines that give other pricklebacks their name. This can lead to confusion when trying to identify it using family characteristics alone.
compareHints: As the only Lumpenus species regularly found in New England waters, snakeblennies are most similar to other prickleback family members like gunnels. However, snakeblennies are much more elongated and snake-like than the flatter, more compressed gunnels, and they lack the distinctive row of pale spots that many gunnels display along their sides.
